{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "mixed", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://www.spring.org.uk/2023/02/what-percentage-communication-nonverbal.php", "note": "Describes the 93% figure as \"a myth deriving from studies by Albert Mehrabian\" when applied to all communication."}, {"claim_snippet": "Research by Albert Mehrabian showed", "source_url": "https://cornerstone.lib.mnsu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=ctamj", "note": "Notes Mehrabian's own stated purpose was to 'find out how well people can judge the feelings of others,' not to measure all communication."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% of all human communication is nonverbal", "source_url": "https://maestrogroup.co/communication-myth/", "note": "Quotes Mehrabian saying, \"it is absurd to imply or suggest that the verbal portion of all communication constitutes only seven percent of the message.\""}, {"claim_snippet": "7%, 38%, 55% breakdown underlying the 93% figure", "source_url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Mehrabian", "note": "Confirms the origin as the '7%-38%-55% Rule' from two 1967 studies on judging feelings/attitudes, not general communication."}, {"claim_snippet": "93% nonverbal", "source_url": "https://drnovak.medium.com/killing-the-myth-that-93-of-communication-is-nonverbal-9603e5e6f939", "note": "States the studies used only 137 college undergraduates, a narrow, non-representative sample, judging inconsistent emotional messages."}], "origin_trace": "Mehrabian & Ferris (1967) and related 1967 studies used small samples of college undergraduates to examine how people judge a speaker's feelings/attitudes when verbal, vocal, and facial cues are inconsistent, producing the 7%-38%-55% breakdown; this was never intended to describe 'all human communication.'", "reasoning": "The 7/38/55 percentages do trace back to real Mehrabian studies, so the figure itself is not fabricated, but the claim vastly overextends its scope: the original research concerned only judgments of feelings/attitudes under conditions of verbal-nonverbal incongruity in a small student sample, not communication in general. Mehrabian himself explicitly rejected the broad interpretation as absurd, and multiple academic and journalistic sources label the 'all communication' framing a persistent myth. Because the number is real but the claim's population, context, and universality are distorted, this is a mixed verdict with high confidence given multiple corroborating primary and secondary sources."}

{"tier": "statistical_data", "verdict": "not supported", "confidence": "high", "evidence": [{"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://time.com/2992051/women-talk-more-study/", "note": "A University of Pennsylvania researcher tracing this figure found it \"may have come from a 1993 marriage counselor's pamphlet\" that was unsourced, not a scientific study."}, {"claim_snippet": "women speak about 20,000 words a day while men speak only about 7,000", "source_url": "https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/women-talk-more-than-men/", "note": "Notes the figure was popularized by Louann Brizendine's 'The Female Brain' (2006), which claimed women speak '20,000 words per day, nearly three times the mere 7,000 spoken by men'; a rigorous Science study found this false."}, {"claim_snippet": "20,000 vs 7,000 words per day", "source_url": "https://www.npr.org/2007/07/05/11762186/study-men-talk-just-as-much-as-women", "note": "The 2007 Science study by Mehl et al. The first real scientific test, Mehl et al.'s 2007 study published in Science (396 college students, recorded via wearable devices), found women averaged ~16,215 words/day and men ~15,669 \u2014 essentially no significant difference, directly contradicting the claim.", "reasoning": "The claim attributes a specific 'study' finding a large gender gap (20,000 vs 7,000 words/day), but no legitimate study supports this; the number traces to an unsourced 1990s self-help pamphlet and was popularized by a non-peer-reviewed book. Because the figure is not merely reframed but empirically contradicted by the best available primary research, and its origin is untraceable to any credible study, the claim is not supported."}
